Examples include spray paint hiss, stake placement, string pulling, tape measure snap, shovel impacts, grass cutting, sod lifting, dirt scraping, wheelbarrow movement, gravel pouring, paver placement, deck board movement, saw cutting, drill fastening, hammering, sanding, stone scraping, concrete mixing by hand, hose water, small pump water, fire pit ignition, outdoor lighting clicks, furniture movement, planters sliding, footsteps, birds, wind through trees, neighborhood ambience, and subtle evening backyard ambience. Sound must always match the exact visible action.

rules: The output must be vertical 9:16 and visually upright, not sideways.
The series hook is: Day X of posting AI until someone actually does it.

The day number must be determined from memory: if previous topic summaries contain Day numbers, use the highest Day number plus one; otherwise use the number of previous completed memory items plus one; if there is no memory, use Day 1.
The chosen day number must be stated in the scene plan and used consistently in overlays and metadata.

CRITICAL OVERLAY DAY NUMBER RULE: The planner must output the chosen Day number as a dedicated field or clearly labeled value at the very top of the scene plan so that overlay generation can extract it. The opening overlay MUST use this exact Day number. The overlay AI agent receives the full scene plan as context — it must read the Day number from the plan and use it verbatim. The Day number in the overlay must ALWAYS match the Day number in the scene plan and metadata title. If the plan says Day 14, the overlay must say DAY 14, not DAY 1.
Generated image/video frames must never contain embedded text, numbers, subtitles, captions, labels, logos, or watermarks. The Day X hook is overlay text only.
The project must be built or transformed by exactly one adult worker only.
The worker may be a man or woman and may be from any ethnicity. The planner should randomize the worker identity across runs without stereotypes.
Maintain the same worker identity, approximate age, body scale, clothing logic, and tool continuity across all scenes in a single video.
Never show multiple workers, assistants, crowds, clients, family members helping, or a construction crew.
Never show heavy machinery, industrial construction equipment, trucks, cranes, forklifts, excavators, bulldozers, loaders, or large delivery vehicles.
All tools and construction methods must be believable for a one-person residential backyard transformation.
The final backyard transformation must feel luxurious, desirable, and almost buildable, not impossible sci-fi or fantasy.
Do not create a giant mansion, full house, skyscraper, massive resort, impossible cliff villa, floating structure, or anything beyond a residential backyard scale.
K0 is the only fully untouched starting-state frame. Scene 1 must not duplicate K0.
K0 must show a plain empty backyard with no construction activity, no tools, no layout marks, no staged materials, and no luxury transformation yet.
Scene 1 must show the first visible construction activity: layout marking, measuring, clearing, or preparing the exact transformation zone.
Every scene must show a clear before-and-after change across the whole work area.
Each scene must have a clearly different start state and end state. No duplicate build stages between consecutive scenes.
The transformation must progress logically from empty backyard to marked layout to groundwork to primary structure to premium finishes to furnishing/styling to final reveal.
The camera must be a wide static vertical backyard view from a slightly elevated angle looking down gently over the full transformation zone.
All scenes must preserve the same camera height, tilt, angle, horizon placement, lens feel, and framing.
Do not use close-up exterior camera framing.
Do not simulate handheld footage, drone shots, orbiting, push-ins, zooms, pans, tilts, dolly moves, tracking shots, reframing, lens changes, or camera shake.
The camera must produce absolutely zero vibration, shake, jitter, wobble, drift, or micro-movement in every frame.
Once the backyard is established in K0, the exact same property must remain locked for the entire sequence.

The backyard identity is fixed: fence layout, neighboring houses, house wall, shed placement, pool or water feature position, patio shape, lawn shape, trees, garden beds, and other major landmarks must not change between scenes.
The work zone must stay in the same screen position across all exterior scenes.
Do not start in a random natural location, commercial resort, public park, empty field, remote wilderness, or unrealistic luxury estate unrelated to the backyard.
The location must be a real residential backyard or compact residential outdoor space.
Each project must include unique environmental elements and backyard context so different videos feel visually distinct and original.
The worker's first action must be directly related to transforming the exact backyard zone.
The worker must never begin with unrelated activity such as playing with a dog, gardening unrelated to the build, relaxing, talking, or walking around aimlessly.
Construction progress must come from continuous repeated manual actions played back quickly, not from magical appearance of objects.
The main visible event in every clip must be the environment transforming, not the worker's body motion alone.
Nothing may appear by magic. Decking, pavers, gravel, edging, water features, fire features, pergolas, lighting, plants, furniture, and decor must arrive and be installed in visible stages.
All materials must obey gravity, weight, support, scale, water flow, fire safety, and residential construction logic.
No floating objects, impossible cantilevers, impossible pools, magical lighting, teleporting furniture, or unrealistic scale jumps.
Water features, plunge pools, spas, or fountains must be small, residential, structurally plausible, and supported by solid ground.
Fire features must be small, controlled, and residential, such as a fire bowl, linear fire pit, or contained fire table.

If an existing pool is visible, the new build area must be clearly separate from it unless the chosen concept is a poolside terrace that remains on solid ground. Nothing may float unsupported on water.
The final result must be a finished luxury backyard space with visible premium materials, lighting, seating, landscaping, and at least one memorable signature feature.
Passive background life may appear, but it must stay subtle, secondary, and unrelated to the worker's actions.
The worker must never interact with background life or stop the build for a side story.
All clips must feel like real continuous construction footage played back at accelerated speed, not a jumpy artificial timelapse or render morph.
Never include multiple shots inside a single generated clip or image.
Never generate an image containing multiple frames, panels, sub-images, split views, storyboard grids, comic-strip layouts, triptychs, before-and-after comparisons, or any multi-frame composition.
Every generated image must be exactly one single continuous photographic frame showing one moment from one camera angle.

CRITICAL 6-SCENE STRUCTURE: This video must have exactly 6 scenes after K0. Scene 1 = layout and first preparation. Scene 2 = groundwork and base formation. Scene 3 = primary structure installation. Scene 4 = premium finishes and systems. Scene 5 = furniture, planting, decor, and final polishing. Scene 6 = final detail work into fully finished luxury reveal.

SCENE-BY-SCENE MANDATORY PROGRESSION: K0 = plain empty untouched backyard. Scene 1/K1 = layout marked and first prep visible. Scene 2/K2 = ground transformed into prepared base, paver bed, deck foundation, or shaped construction zone. Scene 3/K3 = main luxury structure or feature built in rough form. Scene 4/K4 = premium surfaces, lighting, water/fire/feature systems, and landscaping installed. Scene 5/K5 = furniture, plants, decor, and final styling mostly in place. Scene 6/K6 = fully finished luxury backyard reveal with lights, water/fire feature, seating, and polished design.

CRITICAL ORIGINALITY: The planner must NEVER repeat a concept from the last 10 runs. Each episode must feature a genuinely different and surprising backyard transformation idea. Prioritize concepts that are unexpected, inventive, and conversation-starting over safe or conventional luxury patio builds. Think beyond standard fire pits, pergolas, and outdoor kitchens. Consider unusual concepts like: a backyard Japanese onsen soaking garden, a sunken amphitheater with tiered stone seating, a Moroccan riad-style courtyard with mosaic fountain, a hidden speakeasy garden bar behind a living wall, a floating deck island over a dry creek bed, a sculptural concrete wave lounge, a mirrored infinity edge reflecting pool, a hobbit-hole reading nook built into a hillside, a cantilevered observation deck over a slope, a bioluminescent-inspired glow garden with fiber optic paths, a Viking-style longhouse outdoor dining hall, a terraced waterfall meditation garden, a greenhouse cocktail lounge, a suspended hammock lounge between timber posts, or a desert canyon-inspired sunken fire court. The concept must still be residential-scale, physically plausible for one worker, and almost buildable.
global.style_notes: Photorealistic live-action documentary realism with aspirational luxury backyard design. Strict vertical short-form composition. The video should feel like a real one-person backyard transformation recorded from a locked tripod, not like a render showcase, not like a slideshow, and not like generic AI architecture. The visual sweet spot is rich-person realistic: luxurious, surprising, desirable, and almost buildable by a determined individual using hand tools, portable tools, staged materials, and believable small-scale construction methods. memory.instruction:
Use the previous topic summaries as the official series history. First determine the next Day number. If any previous topic summary includes a phrase like Day 12, use the highest detected day number plus one. If no day numbers are present, use the count of previous completed memory items plus one. If memory is empty, this is Day 1. State the exact chosen Day number at the top of the plan.

CRITICAL: The chosen Day number MUST be used consistently everywhere — in the scene plan header, in all overlay text generation, and in all metadata. The overlay system reads the scene plan to extract the Day number. Make the Day number unmistakably clear at the very top of the plan in a format like: SELECTED DAY NUMBER: Day {N}

CRITICAL ANTI-REPETITION: Review ALL previous topic summaries carefully. Do not reuse the same luxury backyard concept, signature feature, layout, material palette, starting yard context, or narrative voice from ANY of the last 10 runs. If the last two runs were fire-related concepts (fire pits, fire lounges, fire features as the primary concept), you MUST choose a concept that does NOT center on fire. Similarly, if recent runs share any common theme (water features, pergolas, outdoor kitchens, etc.), actively avoid that theme.

CRITICAL CREATIVITY MANDATE: Each new episode must feature a concept that is genuinely surprising, inventive, and unlike anything in the series history. Do not default to safe, conventional luxury patio builds. Push for concepts that are extraordinary and conversation-starting while remaining residential-scale and almost buildable. Think of concepts viewers have never seen before in a backyard transformation video. The goal is to make viewers stop scrolling because the idea itself is wild.

Each topic summary should be treated as a previous episode. The new video must feel like a fresh Day in the same challenge series with a dramatically different concept from recent episodes.

camera_rules: Keep the camera completely static with absolutely zero vibration, zero shake, zero jitter, zero wobble, zero drift, and zero micro-movement.
Treat the camera as locked on a tripod bolted to an immovable concrete foundation.
Use a wider vertical 9:16 shot from a slightly elevated viewpoint looking down at a gentle angle over the full backyard transformation zone.
Do not use close-up exterior view.
No camera drift, no handheld motion, no orbiting, no panning, no tilting, no zooming, no dolly, no push-in, no tracking, no reframing, no lens change.

motion_rules: Motion must clearly feel like real continuous backyard construction footage played back at accelerated speed.
Only one adult worker may move in the scene.
No machines may move because no heavy machines may appear.
The worker's motion must always be directly related to the transformation.
The worker should perform continuous repeated manual actions in believable continuity, not isolated poses separated by magical changes.
The dominant visual effect in every clip must be environmental transformation across the whole work area, not just the worker moving.
Scene 1 must show active layout marking or first preparation: measuring, stakes, string, spray paint, chalk, tape, clearing, or outlining the future design.
Scene 2 must show groundwork and base formation: clearing, leveling, gravel spreading, edge restraint placement, paver base, deck footings, shallow trenching, or foundation grid.
Scene 3 must show the main structure or signature feature being assembled in rough form with visible manual progress.
Scene 4 must show premium finishes and systems being installed: pavers, decking, tile, cladding, planters, lighting, water feature, fire feature, privacy screens, or built-in surfaces.
Scene 5 must show furniture, plants, cushions, rugs, decor, and final styling being moved and arranged by the single worker.
Scene 6 must show final detail work and activation into the finished reveal: lights turn on, water/fire feature works, seating is arranged, and the yard looks complete.
Avoid repetitive wandering, idle repositioning, or low-progress action where the site barely changes.
Materials must not teleport or appear fully finished without visible installation stages.
Furniture and decor must be physically moved into place, not appear instantly.
Decks, platforms, pergolas, screens, planters, walls, pavers, and features must be visibly supported and grounded.
Water must flow, fill, or circulate believably; no impossible water physics.
Fire must be contained and residential-scale; no unsafe flames or smoke dominating the scene.
Lighting may activate near the final reveal, but fixtures must be visibly installed before activation.
Passive background-life motion may occur, such as leaves moving, birds crossing, a dog in the far background, pool ripples, or lights turning on, but it must remain secondary.
Do not create impossible transitions where the backyard becomes a different property.
Respect gravity, material weight, support logic, drainage, scale, and real residential construction behavior.
No morphing, melting, teleportation, unstable geometry, or render-like transformation effects.
Do not animate camera motion to compensate for mismatched keyframes.
No generated frame or clip may contain embedded text, numbers, logos, captions, subtitles, or watermarks.
Every scene must have a different start state and end state. No duplicate stages allowed.

CRITICAL STRUCTURE: K0 is generated automatically before your scenes. K0 shows the plain empty untouched backyard with zero construction activity. You do NOT plan K0. CRITICAL REALISM: The final concept should be rich-person realistic and almost buildable. It can be ambitious and luxurious, but it must remain residential backyard scale and physically plausible. No heavy machinery, no giant resort, no impossible mansion, no floating structures, no sci-fi fantasy, no magic appearance of materials.
